summary: The Hypertext Jeopardy Protocol (HTJP) inverts HTTP's request/response semantics: the client sends an answer and expects the server to reply with a correct question. This document is a humorous April 1 RFC, published as informational.

eli5.summary: Like the quiz show where you get the answer and must say the question, the web works backward. You send an answer, and the server must reply with a question.

questions: why is htjp a security risk
subtitle: The web protocol where you send answers and the server provides the questions.

tldr.problem: HTTP works by sending a request and expecting an answer, but someone wondered what if you did it backwards?
tldr.mechanism: HTJP inverts HTTP semantics: the client sends an HTTP response (the answer) and the server replies with an HTTP request (the question that would produce that answer).
tldr.outcome: This April 1st RFC is a humorous thought experiment published for informational purposes. It demonstrates an idea that is valid HTTP but impractical for real deployment.

today: RFC 8565 is an April Fools joke published for informational purposes. It is not intended for implementation and has not been adopted in production systems.

sections.title: The Inverted Protocol
sections.content:
HTJP is a humorous April Fools RFC that describes the Hypertext Jeopardy Protocol, a semantic inverse of HTTP. Instead of the usual convention where a client sends an HTTP request and the server sends an HTTP response, HTJP flips this around: the client sends what would normally be an HTTP response, and the server replies with an HTTP request that, if issued to the appropriate server, would produce the response the client just sent.

The key insight is that both HTTP requests and HTTP responses use the same message format, and it is only convention that clients send requests and servers send responses. HTJP exploits this to create a valid but inverted conversation.
sections.eli5: HTJP takes normal web messages and swaps who sends what. It is still real web traffic, just used backward. Think of it like speaking English backwards: every word is real, but the sentences make no sense.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
An HTJP client sends an HTTP response message as its request. This response contains everything that would normally come from a server: a status line like HTTP/1.1 200 OK, headers, and a body.

The HTJP server receives this and must construct an HTTP request that, if sent to the proper HTTP server, would elicit that exact response. For example, if the client sends a response indicating it came from GET /hello.txt, the server must respond with GET /hello.txt HTTP/1.1 and the appropriate headers.
sections.eli5: You send a message that looks like a normal web answer. The server's job is to figure out what question would get that answer, then send that question back to you.

sections.title: Why This Is Interesting and Dangerous
sections.content:
HTJP reveals an interesting security issue: if a response is predictable, you can use HTJP to reverse-engineer the request that produced it, including any authorization tokens, cookies, or credentials embedded in it. For example, if you send the HTJP server a response that came from an authorized request, the server must reply with an HTTP request containing the credentials that were needed to get that response.

The RFC proposes a defense: servers can add an Anti-HTJP-Nonce header with a random value to responses accessed via authorization. This makes the response unpredictable, so HTJP cannot reverse-engineer the original request. HTJP also works over encrypted connections (called HTJPS), though the security model differs from HTTPS because the hostname in HTJP messages may refer to a different server.
sections.eli5: If you use HTJP to ask for the question behind a secret answer, the server has to give you the secret password that was used. To stop this, servers can add random noise to responses so you cannot use HTJP to steal secrets.

sections.title: Deployment and Reality
sections.content:
HTJP is not meant for production use. The RFC estimates that 0.0% of HTTP proxies and caches support it correctly. Real HTJP deployment would break with most intermediaries because they expect the normal HTTP convention. The RFC is informational, intended to amuse and to illustrate ideas about how protocol semantics work, not to be implemented in actual systems.

The document also describes a meta-joke: the Hypertext Double Jeopardy Protocol (HTJ2P), which inverts HTJP back to normal HTTP, demonstrating that you can keep flipping the semantics indefinitely.
sections.eli5: Nobody actually uses HTJP on the real internet. It is a funny idea that shows how web protocols really work, but the web is not set up for talking backwards.
